Title: Marking on Air-Conditioning and Refrigeration Equipment

Title: Mechanical Execution of Work
Our paraphrase: Install electrical equipment tidily, with good workmanship.

Title: Electrical Connections
Our paraphrase: Connectors and lugs must suit the conductor material, since different metals behave differently, and be installed and used correctly.

Title: Terminals
Our paraphrase: Terminate conductors securely, without nicking or crushing them, by means of pressure connectors, soldered lugs, or splices onto flexible leads.

Title: Working Space - Minimum Clear Distances
Our paraphrase: Working space in front of live parts must be at least as deep as Table 110.26(A)(1) gives, unless exception (a) or (b) applies.

Title: Working Space - Width
Our paraphrase: The clear area in front of equipment must be 30 inches wide at minimum, or as wide as the equipment itself if that is more.

Title: Working Space - Height
Our paraphrase: Working space stays clear from floor, grade or platform level upward, to 6-1/2 ft or to the top of the equipment if that is taller.

Title: GFCI Protection - Dwelling Units
Our paraphrase: Receptacles rated 125 V to 250 V in any dwelling location named in 210.8(A)(1) through (A)(11) require GFCI protection to keep people safe.

Title: GFCI Protection - Bathrooms
Our paraphrase: In a home's bathrooms, every 125 V to 250 V receptacle needs GFCI protection.

Title: GFCI Protection - Garages and Accessory Buildings
Our paraphrase: Garages and outbuildings need GFCI protection on 125 V to 250 V receptacles when the floor is at or below grade.

Title: GFCI Protection - Kitchens
Our paraphrase: In a home's kitchens, receptacles of 125 V to 250 V need GFCI protection, not only the ones that serve the countertop.

Title: GFCI Protection - Laundry Areas
Our paraphrase: Laundry-area receptacles (125 V to 250 V) in a home need GFCI protection.

Title: Branch Circuits Required - Kitchen Small Appliance
Our paraphrase: Besides the circuits required elsewhere in this section, add two or more 20 A small-appliance circuits for the kitchen receptacles.

Title: Branch Circuits Required - Laundry
Our paraphrase: Besides the circuits required elsewhere in this section, add at least one 120 V, 20 A circuit for the laundry receptacle.

Title: Branch Circuits Required - Bathroom
Our paraphrase: Besides the circuits required elsewhere in this section, add at least one 120 V, 20 A circuit for the bathroom receptacles.

Title: AFCI Protection - Dwelling Units
Our paraphrase: In a home, 120 V single-phase 15 A and 20 A branch circuits that serve outlets in habitable rooms such as kitchens, living and dining rooms, bedrooms, closets, hallways and laundry areas need arc-fault protection by one of the methods in 210.12(A)(1) through (A)(6).

Title: Receptacle Outlets Required - General
Our paraphrase: In kitchens, family and dining rooms, living rooms, parlors, libraries, dens, sunrooms, bedrooms, recreation rooms and similar spaces of a home, place receptacles so every point along a wall's floor line is within 6 feet of one.

Title: Receptacle Outlets Required - Small Appliance
Our paraphrase: Kitchen, pantry, breakfast-room and dining-room areas need their wall, floor and countertop receptacles (those covered by 210.52(A) and 210.52(C)), plus receptacles for refrigeration equipment, supplied by the two or more 20 A small-appliance circuits from 210.11(C)(1).

Title: Receptacle Outlets Required - Countertops
Our paraphrase: Countertop receptacles in kitchens, pantries, breakfast and dining areas must be spaced so you are never farther than 24 inches from one, counted horizontally along the wall line.

Title: Lighting Loads for Specified Occupancies
Our paraphrase: Lighting load is at least the unit load in Table 220.12 for the occupancy.

Title: General Calculations - Services and Feeders
Our paraphrase: A feeder or service load must equal at least the sum of the branch-circuit loads it supplies (Part II), after any demand factors allowed by Part III or IV.

Title: Optional Calculation - Dwelling Unit
Our paraphrase: A one-family dwelling, or one unit of a two-family or multifamily dwelling, may use the optional calculation in 220.82: the first 10 kVA of general loads at 100% and the rest at 40%, with heating and air-conditioning loads added by their own percentages.

Title: Service Disconnect - Location
Our paraphrase: Put the service disconnect where it is readily accessible, outside the building or inside near where the service conductors enter.

Title: Rating of Service Disconnecting Means
Our paraphrase: The service disconnect's rating must be at least the calculated load it serves.

Title: Protection of Conductors
Our paraphrase: Overcurrent protection must match each conductor's ampacity (this does not cover flexible cords and cables or fixture wires).

Title: Small Conductors
Our paraphrase: Breaker limits for small conductors, unless 240.4(E) or 240.4(G) allow more. Copper: 14 AWG 15 A, 12 AWG 20 A, 10 AWG 30 A. Aluminum or copper-clad aluminum: 12 AWG 15 A, 10 AWG 25 A.

Title: Overcurrent Device Location - Accessibility
Our paraphrase: Keep breakers and switches within easy reach: with the handle raised to its top position, the middle of its grip must be no higher than 6 ft 7 in. (2.0 m) off the floor or working platform.

Title: General Requirements - Grounding of Electrical Systems
Our paraphrase: Grounding a system ties it to earth to hold down surge voltages (from lightning, line surges, or an accidental touch of higher-voltage lines) and to keep voltage to earth stable during normal use.

Title: Grounding Electrode Conductor Connection
Our paraphrase: The grounding electrode conductor is the link between the grounding electrode(s) and the service's equipment grounding conductors and enclosures and, if the system is grounded, its grounded conductor.

Title: Grounding Electrode System
Our paraphrase: Bond together every electrode of the types listed in 250.52(A)(1) through (A)(7) at a building so they act as one system.

Title: Grounding Electrodes - Metal Underground Water Pipe
Our paraphrase: A metal underground water pipe counts as an electrode when 10 feet or more of it touches the earth, including bonded metal well casing in contact with earth.

Title: Grounding Electrodes - Ground Rod
Our paraphrase: A ground rod needs a length of at least 8 feet and a diameter of at least 5/8 inch (1/2 inch is allowed for listed stainless or nonferrous rods).

Title: Grounding Electrode Conductor Installation - Aluminum
Our paraphrase: Aluminum grounding electrode conductors, whether bare or copper-clad, are off limits where they would touch masonry or soil directly or sit in a corrosive environment.

Title: Bonding of Piping Systems - Metal Water Piping
Our paraphrase: Bond the metal water pipe system to any one of these: the service enclosure, the service's grounded conductor, a grounding electrode conductor of adequate size, or the electrodes in use.

Title: Size of Equipment Grounding Conductors
Our paraphrase: Wire-type equipment grounding conductors are at least the size Table 250.122 specifies.

Title: Conductor Ampacities
Our paraphrase: Conductor ampacities come from Tables 310.16 through 310.21 and their notes.

Title: Ampacities of Insulated Conductors
Our paraphrase: Insulated conductors rated 2000 V or below have their allowable ampacities listed in Table 310.16, which assumes a 30 degrees C ambient.

Title: NM Cable - Uses Permitted
Our paraphrase: Houses and duplexes, their garages and storage buildings (attached or detached), and multifamily dwellings can all use NM, NMC and NMS cable.

Title: NM Cable - Securing and Supporting
Our paraphrase: Fasten NM cable with staples, ties, straps, hangers or the like every 4-1/2 ft or less, and within 12 inches of each cabinet, box or fitting.

Title: Circuit Directory or Circuit Identification
Our paraphrase: Label every circuit, and every change to a circuit, clearly with its specific purpose, in enough detail to tell it apart from all others.

Title: Maximum Number of Overcurrent Devices
Our paraphrase: In addition to 408.30, a panelboard must physically prevent installing more overcurrent devices than the number it was designed, rated and listed for.

Title: Appliances - Flexible Cords
Our paraphrase: Flexible cord may connect appliances that are swapped often or that need noise or vibration isolation.

Title: Motor Branch-Circuit Short-Circuit and Ground-Fault Protection
Our paraphrase: Short-circuit and ground-fault protection for a motor branch circuit has to satisfy 430.52(B) and one of 430.52(C) or (D); the device rating or setting cannot go above the Table 430.52 values.

Title: GFCI Protection - Outdoors
Our paraphrase: Outdoor 125 V to 250 V receptacles at a home need GFCI protection, for example on porches, patios and decks.

Title: GFCI Protection - Bathtubs and Shower Stalls
Our paraphrase: Receptacles of 125 V to 250 V within 6 ft of a tub's or shower's outer edge need GFCI protection.

Title: GFCI Protection - Specific Appliances
Our paraphrase: The outlets that supply dishwashers in homes need GFCI protection, whether the dishwasher is plugged in or hard-wired.

Title: AFCI Protection - Branch Circuit Extensions or Modifications
Our paraphrase: Wiring changes, replacements or extensions on a circuit in the 210.12(B) areas bring the circuit under the same arc-fault protection methods, 210.12(A)(1) through (A)(6).

Title: Receptacle Outlets - Island and Peninsular Countertop Spaces
Our paraphrase: Install at least one receptacle on every island or peninsula countertop that measures 24 inches or more on its long side and 12 inches or more on its short side (islands are covered by (C)(2), peninsulas by (C)(3)).

Title: Receptacle Outlets - Bathrooms
Our paraphrase: A bathroom needs a receptacle no more than 36 inches from the outer edge of each basin, mounted on an adjoining wall or partition, or on the basin cabinet's side or front no lower than 12 inches under the countertop.

Title: Receptacle Outlets - Outdoor Outlets for Dwelling Units
Our paraphrase: At a one-family house, and at every grade-level dwelling unit of a duplex, install at least two outdoor receptacles, front and back, within reach from the ground and no more than 6-1/2 ft above it.

Title: Receptacle Outlets - Basements, Garages, and Accessory Buildings
Our paraphrase: A one-family home needs at least one receptacle in each garage, attached or detached, and in each powered accessory building, and another in an unfinished basement area beyond any laundry receptacles.

Title: Next Higher Standard Overcurrent Device
Our paraphrase: When a conductor's ampacity does not land on a standard device rating from 240.6(A), the next size up may be used, but not for a circuit with more than one receptacle for portable cord-and-plug loads.

Title: NM Cable - Ampacity
Our paraphrase: Where more than two NM cables (each with at least two current-carrying conductors) pass without spacing through the same hole in wood framing that is sealed with insulation, caulk or foam, derate each conductor's ampacity per Table 310.15(C)(1); the adjustment counts only current-carrying conductors.

Title: General Lighting Demand Factors
Our paraphrase: Table 220.42 demand factors apply to the general-illumination part of the branch-circuit load but not to heavy-duty lampholders. In dwellings: 100% for the first 3,000 VA, 35% for VA from 3,001 up to 120,000, and 25% above 120,000 VA.

Title: Supplemental Electrode Required
Our paraphrase: One rod, pipe or plate on its own must be backed by another electrode of a type in 250.52(A)(2) through (A)(8). The extra electrode may be bonded to the first, to the grounding electrode conductor, to the incoming grounded conductor at the service, or to the service enclosure. Exception: a lone electrode that measures 25 ohms or less to earth needs no supplement.

Title: Intersystem Bonding Termination
Our paraphrase: Provide an intersystem bonding termination outside enclosures at the service or metering enclosure and at the disconnect of any additional building or structure; it needs terminals for at least three intersystem bonding conductors.

Title: Means of Identifying Grounded Conductors
Our paraphrase: Insulated grounded conductors of 6 AWG or smaller are marked along their whole length with a solid white or gray finish, or with stripes (three, continuous, white or gray) on insulation that is not green.

Title: Rating
Our paraphrase: A branch circuit's rating equals the maximum ampere rating or setting allowed for its overcurrent device; circuits that are not individual circuits use 15, 20, 30, 40 or 50 A.

Title: Branch-Circuit Conductors - Minimum Ampacity
Our paraphrase: Branch-circuit conductors must carry at least the largest load they serve; size them to the greater of the results from 210.19(A)(1) and (A)(2).

Title: Minimum Rating and Size of Feeders
Our paraphrase: Feeder conductors must carry the load found by the Article 220 calculation parts III, IV and V. Before any adjustment or correction factors, the smallest allowable conductor must be rated to carry the noncontinuous load together with 125 percent of what runs continuously.

Title: Other Loads - All Occupancies
Our paraphrase: Outside dwelling units, count at least 180 VA for each single or multiple receptacle on one yoke, and for other outlets that are not part of general lighting. A dwelling does not count its receptacles one by one, because they are covered by the general lighting load.

Title: Receptacle Loads - Other Than Dwelling Units
Our paraphrase: Receptacle loads from 220.14 may use the Table 220.44 demand factors or be calculated as 220.44(A) allows.

Title: Feeder Taps Not Over 10 ft
Our paraphrase: A tap off a feeder needs no overcurrent device where it connects if all of these hold: it is 3.0 m (10 ft) long or less; its ampacity covers the calculated loads it feeds and is at least the rating of the equipment or device it ends at; it does not extend past that equipment; it is enclosed in a raceway; and a tap that leaves the enclosure has an ampacity of at least 10 percent of the feeder device rating.

Title: Effective Ground-Fault Current Path
Our paraphrase: Equipment, wiring and other conductive material that could become energized must be installed to form a low-impedance path that helps the overcurrent device operate.

Title: Types of Equipment Grounding Conductors
Our paraphrase: The equipment grounding conductor that accompanies or surrounds the circuit conductors can be aluminum, copper, or copper-clad aluminum wire, or a raceway type: rigid or intermediate metal conduit, EMT or listed flexible metal conduit (other listed types also qualify).

Title: Protection Against Physical Damage - Cables Through Framing Members
Our paraphrase: When cable or a raceway runs through holes drilled in joists, rafters or other wood framing (exposed or concealed), keep at least 1-1/4 in. (32 mm) between the hole and the wood's nearest edge. If you cannot, shield the cable or raceway against screws and nails with a steel plate or bushing.

Title: Underground Installations
Our paraphrase: Direct-buried cables and raceways must meet the minimum cover in Table 300.5. Underground cables beneath a building go in a raceway. Protect underground conductors from damage as 300.5(D) describes.

Title: Number of Conductors in Outlet, Device, and Junction Boxes
Our paraphrase: Choose a box or conduit body big enough to leave free space for every conductor inside; the box volume must at least match the fill calculation in 314.16(A) and (B). Count a conductor once if it begins outside and ends or is spliced inside, and once if it simply passes through without splice or termination.

Title: Marking on Motors and Multimotor Equipment
Our paraphrase: A motor nameplate must show the manufacturer, voltage, frequency, number of phases, full-load amps, temperature rise or insulation class, ambient temperature, duty rating, horsepower, and locked-rotor code letter, plus any other specified information.

Title: Single Motor - Branch-Circuit Conductor Size
Our paraphrase: Conductors for one continuously running motor need ampacity of at least 125 percent of its full-load current (taken per 430.6(A)(1)).

Title: Several Motors or a Motor(s) and Other Load(s)
Our paraphrase: For several motors, or a motor plus other loads, conductor ampacity is 125 percent of the largest motor's full-load current plus the full-load currents of the other motors plus the ampacity needed for the other loads.

Title: Continuous-Duty Motors - Overload Protection
Our paraphrase: A continuous-duty motor over 1 hp needs its own overload device that responds to motor current. Set it to trip at no more than 125 percent of nameplate full-load current when the motor has a service factor of 1.15 or more, or a marked temperature rise of 40 C or less, and no more than 115 percent for other motors. If that setting cannot start the motor or carry its load, 430.32(C) allows a higher setting, up to 140 percent and 130 percent.

Title: Motor Controller Disconnecting Means
Our paraphrase: A motor disconnect must be in sight of the motor and of the machinery the motor drives.

Title: Ampere Rating and Interrupting Capacity of Motor Disconnecting Means
Our paraphrase: The disconnect for a motor circuit of 600 V or less must be rated at 115 percent or more of the motor's full-load current. For a Design E motor, mark the disconnect as suitable for a Design E motor.

Title: Receptacle Replacements - GFCI
Our paraphrase: If the receptacle box lacks a grounding means, either a GFCI-type receptacle or a GFCI breaker is an allowed solution.

Title: Motor Ampere Ratings - Table Values
Our paraphrase: Take motor current ratings from Table 430.247, 430.248, 430.249 or 430.250 whenever the rating determines conductor ampacity, switch size, protection of the branch circuit against short circuits and ground faults, or overload protection.

Title: Small-Appliance and Laundry Loads - Dwelling Unit
Our paraphrase: Each 2-wire small-appliance circuit (210.11(C)(1)) and each laundry circuit (210.11(C)(2)) in a dwelling counts as 1,500 VA; add these to the general lighting load if you like and apply the Table 220.42 demand factors to the sum.

Title: Electric Dryer Load - Dwelling Unit
Our paraphrase: A household electric dryer counts as 5,000 W or its nameplate rating, whichever is larger, and Table 220.54 demand factors may be used for multiple dryers.

Title: Electric Cooking Equipment - Dwelling Unit
Our paraphrase: Demand for household electric ranges, built-in wall ovens, countertop cooking units and similar appliances individually rated above 1-3/4 kW may come from Table 220.55. A single circuit feeding a cooking appliance of 12 kW or less is limited to 8 kW of demand.

Title: Optional Calculation - Existing Dwelling Unit
Our paraphrase: An existing dwelling may use an optional method: total the lighting and receptacle load, the load from small-appliance and laundry circuits, and any other nameplate loads, then count the first 8 kVA at 100% and the rest at 40% (when no heating or air-conditioning is being added; added loads change the method).

Title: Installation and Use - Listed or Labeled Equipment
Our paraphrase: Install and use listed or labeled equipment the way its listing or labeling instructions say.

Title: Temperature Limitations
Our paraphrase: Choose conductor ampacity temperature ratings so they do not exceed the lowest rating among the connected terminations, conductors or devices.

Title: Dwelling Unit Receptacle Outlets - Hallways
Our paraphrase: Hallways in homes that run 10 ft (3.0 m) or longer need at least one receptacle.

Title: Size of AC Grounding Electrode Conductor
Our paraphrase: Table 250.66 gives the smallest allowed grounding electrode conductor for a service, for buildings fed from a feeder or a branch circuit, and for a separately derived system.
